lead: A random variable X can be fed into a function g. The result Y=g(X) is itself random: each outcome that gave X=x now gives Y=g(x). Its distribution is inherited from X, not chosen separately. This matters when a meter reports voltage but you need power, when a bank records a ratio, or when a model squares an error. The job is to find the support of Y, then its pmf or pdf. Discrete variables add probabilities of preimages; continuous variables use the CDF or a derivative formula.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.4 for pmf, pdf and CDF, and Chapter 2.5 to check answers by expectation.

blocks.text: Suppose X is discrete with pmf p_X(x)=P(X=x). Fix a real number y. The event Y=y happens exactly when X takes some value x with g(x)=y. Those x values are disjoint, so add their probabilities:
p_Y(y)=Σ_{x:g(x)=y} p_X(x)
blocks.where: p_Y(y) is the pmf of Y; the sum runs over every x in the support of X that maps to y; p_X(x) is the old pmf. If no x maps to y, p_Y(y)=0.

blocks.text: The support is the set {g(x): p_X(x)>0}. Write it every time.

Example: X takes -1, 0, 1 with probability 1/3 each. Y=X². Then y=0 has one preimage x=0, so p_Y(0)=1/3. y=1 has two preimages x=-1 and x=1, so p_Y(1)=1/3+1/3=2/3. Support is {0,1}. All other y have probability 0.

Sort a table of x, p_X(x), g(x) by y and add p_X in each group. The total remains 1. The map y=g(x) need not be one-to-one; two x values can land on the same y. That is why the sum, not a single term, is the definition.
Some syllabi call this transformation of variables. Nothing about X changes; only our description of Y is new.

sections.h3: Continuous case: CDF first, then derivative

blocks.text: For continuous X with pdf f_X, start from the CDF of Y:
F_Y(y)=P(Y≤y)=P(g(X)≤y)
blocks.where: F_Y is the CDF of Y. Solve g(X)≤y for X, use the known CDF of X, then differentiate:

blocks.text: f_Y(y)=d/dy F_Y(y)
blocks.where: f_Y is the pdf of Y.

blocks.text: If g is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on the support, use:
f_Y(y)=f_X(g⁻¹(y)) |d/dy g⁻¹(y)|
blocks.where: g⁻¹(y) is the x that gives g(x)=y; f_X is evaluated at that x; |d/dy g⁻¹(y)| is the absolute derivative of the inverse. The absolute value is needed because a decreasing g reverses intervals but a pdf cannot be negative.

blocks.text: The formula holds only for y in the support of Y. Outside it, f_Y(y)=0. State the support with the formula.

items: Write the support of X and the map y=g(x).
Find the range of g; that is the support of Y.
Check whether g is one-to-one on the support.
If yes, invert x=g⁻¹(y), compute the derivative, substitute, and simplify.
If no, split into monotone branches and add contributions.
Check that the total area is 1.

blocks.text: For non-monotone maps, the direct formula has one term per preimage:
f_Y(y)=Σ_i f_X(x_i(y)) |dx_i/dy|
blocks.where: x_i(y) are the distinct solutions of g(x)=y and dx_i/dy is the derivative of each branch. This is the continuous version of adding preimages. When two variables transform together, the joint distribution needs a Jacobian; that is Unit 4.

sections.h3: Linear maps and two standard nonlinear maps

blocks.text: Linear map Y=aX+b. Here a and b are constants with a≠0. The inverse is x=(y-b)/a and dx/dy=1/a. The formula gives

blocks.where: |a| is the absolute value of a, for y in the range. If X lies in (α,β), then Y lies between aα+b and aβ+b, with endpoints ordered. A positive a preserves order; a negative a flips it. The factor 1/|a| stretches the density upward when |a|<1 (and squeezes it downward when |a|>1), so the total area stays 1.

blocks.text: Square map Y=X². Take X uniform on (0,1), so f_X(x)=1 for 0<x<1. On this support g is increasing. The inverse is x=√y and dx/dy=1/(2√y). Thus

blocks.where: √y is the positive square root. The density blows up near 0 but the area is finite and equals 1. The support is (0,1), not all y≥0.

blocks.text: Square root map Y=√X. With the same X, inverse x=y² and dx/dy=2y. Then f_Y(y)=2y for 0<y<1. Both maps are one-to-one on (0,1), so no branch sum is needed.
A non-monotone case: X symmetric on (-1,1) and Y=X². Each y in (0,1) has two preimages, x=√y and x=-√y. Add both branch contributions; the support starts at 0.

figure.caption: For X uniform on (0,1), the flat density f_X(x)=1 and the derived density f_Y(y)=1/(2√y) for Y=X². Both curves enclose area 1; the derived density is tall near 0.

spec.aria: Plot of the uniform density f_X(x)=1 and the derived density f_Y(y)=1/(2√y) for Y=X²; both have area 1.

examples.question: X is uniform on (0,1), so f_X(x)=1 for 0<x<1. Let Y=X². Find the pdf of Y, state its support, find P(Y≤1/4), and evaluate f_Y(1/4).
steps: Support of X is (0,1). The map y=x² is increasing there, so the range and support of Y are (0,1).
Inverse: x=√y. Derivative: dx/dy=1/(2√y), which is positive.
examples.answer: The pdf is f_Y(y)=1/(2√y) for 0<y<1 and 0 outside; P(Y≤1/4)=0.5; f_Y(1/4)=1.
examples.check:
import math
p = 0.5
y = 0.25
f = 1/(2*math.sqrt(y))
print(p)
print(f)

traps: Omitting the absolute derivative; a decreasing inverse has negative derivative, so the density would come out negative.
Forgetting a second preimage in a non-monotone map, such as Y=X² on a symmetric support.
Writing f_Y(y) for y outside the support; state the range every time.
Treating y=g(x) as one-to-one when it is not; check the support for turning points.
Not checking that the resulting density integrates to 1; this catches missing branches and wrong constants.

quiz.q: State the pmf formula for Y=g(X) when X is discrete.
quiz.a: p_Y(y)=Σ_{x:g(x)=y} p_X(x), summed over all x in the support of X that map to y; p_Y(y)=0 if no such x exists.

quiz.q: Why does the monotone continuous formula use the absolute derivative of the inverse?
quiz.a: A decreasing inverse has a negative derivative. A pdf cannot be negative, so the absolute value keeps the density positive and preserves total area 1.

quiz.q: X is uniform on (0,1). Let Y=√X. Find the pdf and support of Y, and find P(Y≤1/2).
quiz.a: Inverse x=y², dx/dy=2y, so f_Y(y)=2y for 0<y<1 and 0 outside. P(Y≤1/2)=P(X≤1/4)=1/4, or ∫_0^{1/2} 2y dy=1/4.

quiz.q: X is uniform on (-1,1), so f_X(x)=1/2 there. Let Y=X². Find the pdf and support of Y.
quiz.a: Support of Y is (0,1). For 0<y<1 there are two preimages x=√y and x=-√y. Each branch contributes (1/2)·1/(2√y), so f_Y(y)=1/(2√y) for 0<y<1 and 0 outside.

quiz.q: X takes -1, 0, 1 with probabilities 0.2, 0.3, 0.5. Let Y=X². Find the pmf of Y.
quiz.a: y=0 has preimage 0, so p_Y(0)=0.3. y=1 has preimages -1 and 1, so p_Y(1)=0.2+0.5=0.7. Support is {0,1}.

quiz.q: If g is monotone decreasing, how does the support of Y relate to the support of X?
quiz.a: The endpoints reverse order. If X lies in (α,β), then Y lies between g(β) and g(α); the formula still uses the absolute derivative.

quiz.q: What is the first step for a continuous transformation Y=g(X)?
quiz.a: Write the support of X and find the range of g; that range is the support of Y. Then use the CDF method or, if g is monotone, the inverse-derivative formula.

quiz.q: X is uniform on (0,1). Let Y=2X+3. Find the pdf and support of Y, and find P(Y≤3.5).
quiz.a: Inverse x=(y-3)/2, dx/dy=1/2, so f_Y(y)=1/2 for 3<y<5 and 0 outside. P(Y≤3.5)=P(X≤0.25)=0.25.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, transformations of random variables are simulated: draw many X values, push them through g, and compare the histogram with the formula. Probabilistic programming languages do this automatically for complex models. The same idea appears in uncertainty propagation and in the delta method for approximate variances. Search next for transformation of random variables, change of variables, pushforward measure, inverse CDF sampling, and delta method.
